question.explanation: ANSWER: (C) is the best answer. 35 U.S.C. § 102; MPEP §§ 2111 and 2131. MPEP § 2131, under the heading, “To Anticipate A Claim, The Reference Must Teach Every Element Of The Claim.” "A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference." See Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil Co. of California, 814 F.2d 628, 631, 2 USPQ2d 1051, 1053 (Fed. Cir. 1987). Here, every element of the claim is found in Patent A. See MPEP 2111, under the heading “Claims Must Be Given Their Broadest Reasonable Interpretation,” where it explained that “[d]uring patent examination, the pending claims must be ‘given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification,” and cites In re Prater, 415 F.2d 1393, 1404-05, 162 USPQ 541, 550-51 (CCPA 1969) to explain that "reading a claim in light of the specification, to thereby interpret limitations explicitly recited in the claim, is a quite different thing from 'reading limitations of the specification into a claim,' to thereby narrow the scope of the claim by implicitly adding disclosed limitations which have no express basis in the claim." (A) and (B) are incorrect. MPEP § 2111. The claim, as written, is not allowable over Patent A since Patent A disclosed every element recited in the claim. (D) is incorrect. There is no need to search again for a building material, this time looking for balsa wood. The claim has not been amended to be directed to balsa wood. Since it still broadly recites “wood,” Patent A that discloses pine remains germane and anticipates the claim. (E) is incorrect for one or more reasons. It is incorrect because it wrongly agrees with the practitioner’s argument that Patent A is poor reference. It also is incorrect because it seeks to reject the claim over 35 U.S.C. § 112(b), for indefiniteness. The claim is clear on its face and there is nothing indefinite about what the claim says. This answer makes the mistake of confusing breadth with indefiniteness. The claim is broad but it is definite.

distractor_analysis.A: The claim, unamended, is still fully anticipated because every element is found in the reference, so allowance isn't warranted.
distractor_analysis.B: Same defect as (A), plus a Reasons for Allowance would be pointless since the claim remains unpatentable as written.
distractor_analysis.D: There's no basis to reopen and search again; the claim hasn't changed, so the existing reference -- which discloses every claimed element under the generic term 'wood' -- remains germane.
distractor_analysis.E: This confuses claim breadth with indefiniteness; a broad-but-clear claim isn't indefinite under §112(b), it's just still anticipated as written.

diagnosis.distinguishing_fact: The claim was never amended to recite 'balsa wood' specifically -- it still broadly recites 'wood,' so under the broadest-reasonable-interpretation standard the pine-disclosing reference continues to anticipate every element of the claim exactly as written, regardless of what the specification emphasizes.
diagnosis.one_line_rule: A claim retains its broadest reasonable interpretation until actually amended; an unamended claim that still reads on a disclosed reference remains anticipated no matter how persuasively the applicant argues around what the specification favors. MPEP §§ 2111, 2131.

question.question: In accordance with the MPEP and USPTO rules and procedure, a registered attorney or agent may be appointed to prosecute a patent application for an applicant. In which of the following situations will the USPTO not recognize the appointment of an attorney or agent to prosecute a patent application for an applicant?

choices.A: The principal agent of record appoints a registered associate attorney to prosecute the application.
choices.B: The applicant executes a power of attorney naming only a law firm to prosecute the application.
choices.C: The applicant executes a power of attorney appointing more than one registered individual to prosecute the application.
choices.D: The principal attorney of record appoints an associate registered agent to prosecute the application.
choices.E: The assignee of the entire interest of record, who has established the right to prosecute the patent application, executes a power of attorney appointing a registered attorney to prosecute the patent application.

question.explanation: ANSWER: Choice (B) is the correct answer. MPEP § 402; 37 C.F.R. § 1.34. MPEP § 402 states that “Powers of attorney or authorizations of agent naming firms of attorneys or agents filed in patent applications will not be recognized.” (A) and (D) are each incorrect because according to 37 C.F.R. § 1.34(b), “A principal registered attorney or agent, so appointed, may appoint an associate registered attorney or agent who shall also then be of record.” (C) is incorrect. As stated in MPEP § 402, “Powers of attorney and authorizations of agent under 37 C.F.R. § 1.34(b) naming one or more registered individuals, or all registered practitioners associated with a Customer Number, may be made. See MPEP § 403 for Customer Number practice.” (E) is incorrect because, as set forth in MPEP § 402.07, “A power of attorney by the assignee of the entire interest revokes all powers given by the applicant and prior assignees if the assignee establishes their right to take action as provided in 37 C.F.R. § 3.73(b).”

distractor_analysis.A: 37 CFR 1.34(b) expressly permits a principal registered attorney to appoint an associate registered attorney, who then also becomes of record.
distractor_analysis.C: MPEP § 402 permits naming one or more registered individuals, or all practitioners under a Customer Number.
distractor_analysis.D: MPEP § 402 likewise permits a principal registered agent to appoint an associate registered agent.
distractor_analysis.E: MPEP § 402.07 expressly permits an assignee of the entire interest, once it has established its right to take action, to execute a power of attorney appointing a registered attorney.

diagnosis.distinguishing_fact: Every scenario naming one or more actual registered individuals -- whether appointed by a principal practitioner, by the applicant, or by the assignee -- is recognized; only naming a firm, with no individual named, is refused under MPEP § 402.
diagnosis.one_line_rule: The USPTO will not recognize a power of attorney or authorization of agent that names only a firm rather than one or more registered individuals. MPEP § 402; 37 CFR 1.34.

question.explanation: ANSWER: (A) is the most correct answer. See 37 CFR § 1.33(c). (B) is incorrect. See MPEP § 403. Powers of attorney to firms filed in executed applications filed after July 2, 1971, are not recognized by the Patent and Trademark Office. However, the firm’s address will be considered to be the correspondence address. (C) is incorrect. See MPEP §§ 402.02 and 406. The associate attorney may not appoint another attorney. (D) is incorrect. 37 CFR § 1.36. An assignment will not itself operate as a revocation of a power or authorization previously given. (E) is incorrect. See MPEP § 402.05. Revocation of the power of the principal attorney or agent revokes powers granted by him or her to other attorneys or agents.

distractor_analysis.B: MPEP § 403 states powers of attorney to firms filed after July 2, 1971 are not recognized (though the firm's address is treated as the correspondence address) -- the opposite of what this choice claims.
distractor_analysis.C: MPEP §§ 402.02 and 406 state an associate attorney may not appoint another attorney; only a principal may make that appointment.
distractor_analysis.D: 37 CFR 1.36 states an assignment does not itself operate as a revocation of a previously given power or authorization.
distractor_analysis.E: MPEP § 402.05 states revocation of the principal's power does revoke powers granted by the principal to other attorneys or agents -- the opposite of what this choice claims.

diagnosis.distinguishing_fact: Only the reexamination-notice rule is stated correctly; each of the other four choices inverts or misstates an actual, specific rule -- firm POAs are not recognized (not the reverse), associates cannot sub-appoint, assignment doesn't itself revoke a POA, and revoking the principal's power does revoke powers he granted to others.
diagnosis.one_line_rule: In a reexamination, notices to the patent owner go to the attorney or agent of record at the address on the register of patent attorneys and agents. 37 CFR 1.33(c).
